title: Hyperion
author: Simmons, Dan
review:
The humanity shines through despite this being in the far future and a world apart from where we are now. It does this in a realistic way, humans still act similar to how they do today but with access to a swathe of futuristic technology that is indistinguishable from magic. The characters are more well done than a lot of other science fiction stories; Simmons is able to portray his vision for the future in multiple distinct perspectives. The structure of this story is really well done and the memoir-like chapters take very unexpected turns and connect to each-other in interesting ways so there's a ton of variety here.

Something that really stood out to me are the elements of horror in the book, the Shrike is very spooky and mysterious, so you also get elements of a great horror novel intermixed with the memoir and sci-fi elements that are wholly unique.

It's also interesting how prominent the alien worlds' fauna and creatures are. The atmosphere of these worlds are all different and dangerous despite how advanced the technology is, our characters can come to harm from the natural forces as well.

My biggest knock against this is it feels like half the book is missing and just ends abruptly, but planning on reading the next book immediately to hopefully get a satisfying conclusion.

highlights.text: I find that even fear fades and becomes commonplace after days of anticlimax.
IN THE BEGINNING was the Word. Then came the fucking word processor. Then came the thought processor. Then came the death of literature. And so it goes.
Francis Bacon once said, “There arises from a bad and unapt formation of words a wonderful obstruction to the mind.”
I love being a poet. It’s the goddamned words I can’t stand.
I waited then. I wait still. The poem must be finished. It will be finished. In the beginning was the Word. In the end…past honor, past life, past caring… In the end will be the Word.
Suffice it to say that I believe the Ousters have done what Web humanity has not in the past millennia: evolved.
For you see, I remember my grandmother’s dream. I remember the way it could have been. I remember Siri.
“I’m creating the future,” he repeated without looking up, “but it’s the past which must be changed. One instant. One decision.”
